title: Why Use A5?
description: A5 is a [pentagonal discrete global grid system](https://a5geo.org/docs/technical/dggs) — an alternative to Uber's [H3](https://h3geo.org/) (hexagonal) and Google's [S2](https://s2geometry.io/) (square). It collapses a `(lon, lat)` point to a single 64-bit integer cell ID you can `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, and index — the same role H3 / S2 IDs play — with the distinguishing property that every cell at a given resolution covers the same area on the globe.

sections.title: Why pentagons, and why equal area
sections.description: A discrete global grid system answers one question: how do you tile a sphere with cells that are roughly the same size everywhere, so that counting points per cell is meaningful? Every system makes a different trade. A5's choice is to keep cell area as uniform as possible across the entire globe, accepting pentagonal cells to get it.
sections.imageAlt: Cell shapes compared: H3 hexagons, S2 squares, and A5 pentagons
sections.imageCaption: A5's pentagons (right) come from a dodecahedral subdivision — no special-case cells, equal area everywhere.

bulletPoints.label: The problem A5 solves
bulletPoints.description: When you bucket `(lon, lat)` points into grid cells and compare counts, the comparison is only honest if the cells are the same size. Grids built on lat/lon rectangles or projected squares stretch badly toward the poles, so a count of 100 near the equator and 100 near a pole describe very different densities. A5 cells are equal-area at each resolution by construction, so cross-latitude density comparisons need no per-cell normalization.

bulletPoints.label: Pentagons are the cost of that uniformity
bulletPoints.description: You cannot tile a sphere with regular hexagons alone — H3 pays for its hexagons with [12 unavoidable pentagon exceptions](https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/coordsystems) at the icosahedral vertices that traversal code must special-case. A5 instead derives its cells from a [dodecahedral subdivision](https://a5geo.org/examples/teohedron-dodecahedron), giving pentagons *everywhere* — uniform shape, uniform area, and no exceptional cells to handle. The geometric argument is laid out on the [A5 motivation page](https://a5geo.org/docs/motivation).

bulletPoints.label: It's a thin binding over the reference library
bulletPoints.description: The DuckDB functions wrap the upstream [A5 Rust library](https://github.com/felixpalmer/a5), so cell IDs are identical to what the reference implementation produces — a DuckDB-computed ID round-trips through the JS/TypeScript library and back unchanged.

sections.title: How a point becomes a cell ID
sections.description: Encoding a coordinate is a deterministic geometric pipeline, and the resulting 64-bit unsigned integer (`UBIGINT`) is self-describing — it carries its own resolution, which is why you never need a separate level column alongside it.

bulletPoints.label: From sphere to cell
bulletPoints.description: A point is located on the globe, mapped onto the face of the dodecahedron it falls in, and then placed within that face's recursive pentagonal subdivision down to the requested resolution. Resolution 0 is the small set of base cells covering the whole globe; each finer level subdivides every cell, so cell count grows by a fixed branching factor per level and resolution 30 reaches sub-square-meter precision.

bulletPoints.label: Resolution is packed into the ID
bulletPoints.description: The cell's position in the subdivision hierarchy *and* its resolution level are encoded together into the single `UBIGINT`. Because the level lives inside the integer, the resolution can be recovered from a bare cell ID with no side table — and a cell at one resolution maps deterministically to its ancestor at any coarser level, which is what makes hierarchical roll-up a pure integer operation rather than a re-encode of the raw points.

bulletPoints.label: Pick the coarsest resolution that still separates your data
bulletPoints.description: Each finer level multiplies the number of distinct cells (and therefore `GROUP BY` cardinality) by the branching factor. Encode once at the finest resolution you'll ever need; roll up to coarser views in-query for free. The [Cookbook](#cookbook) and the resolution guide in the details below show the area-per-level trade-off.

bulletPoints.label: Cells are integers first, geometry on demand
bulletPoints.description: Storage and joins use the compact integer. When you need to *draw* a cell, the boundary is materialized as `[lon, lat]` vertex pairs that pair with the [`spatial`](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/spatial) extension's polygon builders for GeoJSON output — the exact pattern is in the Cookbook.

sections.title: A5 vs H3 vs S2
sections.description: All three are global cell-based spatial indices that produce integer IDs. The shape of the cell, and how uniform its area is across the globe, is what differs — and that difference, plus ecosystem maturity, is the whole decision.

bulletPoints.label: Cell shape
bulletPoints.description: [H3](https://h3geo.org/) tiles the world with hexagons (with 12 unavoidable pentagons at the icosahedral vertices). [S2](https://s2geometry.io/) uses curvilinear quadrilaterals derived from a cube projection. A5 uses **pentagons throughout**, derived from a [dodecahedral subdivision](https://a5geo.org/examples/teohedron-dodecahedron) — see [the A5 motivation page](https://a5geo.org/docs/motivation) for the geometric argument.

bulletPoints.label: Area uniformity
bulletPoints.description: H3 hex area drifts noticeably with latitude — same-resolution cells near the poles are smaller than at the equator. A5 cells are equal-area at each resolution by construction, which matters when you're computing densities or comparing counts across very different latitudes. The [A5 vs H3](https://a5geo.org/docs/recipes/a5-vs-h3) page in the upstream docs walks through the trade.

bulletPoints.label: Neighbor count
bulletPoints.description: Hexagons have a clean 6-neighbor structure that's nice for grid traversal. Pentagons have 5 edge-neighbors, which is slightly less convenient — but A5 has no "pentagon exceptions" the way H3 does, so neighborhood queries don't need special-case logic.

bulletPoints.label: Ecosystem maturity
bulletPoints.description: H3 is older and has a much larger ecosystem (Postgres, BigQuery, Snowflake, Spark, plus Uber's first-party libraries). S2 is widely deployed inside Google. A5 is newer — the upstream library and specification are at [github.com/felixpalmer/a5](https://github.com/felixpalmer/a5). If you need the broadest tool support today, H3 is still the safest pick. Reach for A5 specifically when uniform cell area matters.
